planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in humus-rich to lean, alkaline-tolerant, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; ladder brake fern is remarkably adaptable to poor soils, including limestone rubble and mortar joints in walls.

directions: Plant in humus-rich to lean, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; Chinese ladder brake fern produces upright clumps of narrow, pinnate fronds with closely spaced, ladder-like leaflets. It is exceptionally tolerant of alkaline and even mildly saline or disturbed soils, often naturalizing in old mortar, brick walls, and limestone outcrops where few other ferns survive. In the Gulf South and Florida it has become a vigorous spore-spreading naturalizer and is listed as invasive in parts of the region, so site it where self-sowing is acceptable or remove spent fertile fronds before spores mature. It is also notable among botanists as a documented arsenic-hyperaccumulating species used in phytoremediation research. Best used in warm-zone shaded beds, rock walls, or naturalized woodland edges rather than near sensitive wetlands.
sources: USDA Forest Service invasive species profiles

planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in shade; Australian brake fern grows unusually fast for a fern and benefits from a sheltered, frost-free site or container culture outside zones 9-11.

directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; Australian brake fern forms large, soft-textured clumps of finely divided, lacy, light-green fronds on an upright, arching plant that grows notably faster than most garden ferns, often reaching full size within a single season from a division. Native to Australia and New Zealand, it readily self-sows by spores in warm, humid shade gardens and can seed into nearby pots and beds, so remove spent fronds if volunteer seedlings are unwanted. Its large size and fast growth make it a good quick-fill specimen for new shaded borders or a dramatic backdrop fern behind smaller groundcover ferns. Protect from frost; foliage is damaged below the high 20s F.

planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in moist, humus-rich, acidic, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; rasp fern (formerly classified as Doodia aspera) spreads slowly by rhizomes to form a dense, low groundcover.

directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, acidic, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; rasp fern is a compact Australian and New Zealand native valued for its coarsely textured, rough-to-the-touch (hence 'rasp') fronds that emerge a vivid pink to coppery-red before maturing to deep green, giving a long season of color contrast against plain-green companion ferns. It spreads gradually by short rhizomes into a dense, low clump useful as a textural groundcover at the front of a shaded border, in rockeries, or beneath taller tree ferns. This species was formerly treated as Doodia aspera, and you may still see it sold under that name. It tolerates brief dry spells better than many fine-textured ferns once established.

common_name: Austral Gem Fern (Hybrid Bird's Nest Fern)

planting.note: Plant container plants in spring in moist, humus-rich, well-drained substrate in bright indirect light to deep shade; Austral Gem is a sterile hybrid between bird's nest fern and Norfolk Island spleenwort, prized for its vigor and resistance to leaf-spot disease.

directions: Grow in moist, humus-rich, well-drained substrate in bright indirect light to shade; Austral Gem is a naturally occurring hybrid between bird's nest fern (Asplenium nidus) and Norfolk Island spleenwort (Asplenium dimorphum), combining the broad, glossy, undivided fronds of its nidus parent with the more deeply ruffled, dissected frond margins of dimorphum. It is notably more vigorous and faster-growing than straight Asplenium nidus, and being a sterile hybrid it produces no viable spores, making it a tidy, non-spreading choice for shaded beds in frost-free zones or as a large container and houseplant specimen elsewhere. It is also valued commercially for improved tolerance of the leaf-spot fungal diseases that commonly affect bird's nest fern in humid greenhouse production. Protect from temperatures below 50°F.

planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; comb fern tolerates both terrestrial and epiphytic growing conditions in zones 10-12.

directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; comb fern produces upright to arching fronds with narrow, closely spaced, comb-like leaflets, giving the plant a finer, more erect texture than the familiar Boston fern. Native throughout tropical America, it grows equally well rooted in the ground or perched epiphytically on logs and tree trunks, and tolerates brief waterlogging better than many Nephrolepis species. It makes a good basket or raised-bed specimen in frost-free, humid shade gardens, pairing well with other tropical understory ferns and aroids. Keep substrate consistently moist and provide high humidity for best frond quality.

planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in humus-rich, well-drained soil or as an epiphyte on logs and tree trunks in partial to full shade; kangaroo fern spreads by creeping rhizomes to form a loose groundcover mat.

directions: Plant in humus-rich, well-drained soil or on a mossy log or stump in partial to full shade; kangaroo fern is a creeping New Zealand native that scrambles over rocks, logs, and tree trunks on slender rhizomes, producing simple to shallowly lobed, leathery, glossy green fronds. In the garden it is most effective allowed to ramble over a shaded rock wall, stump, or mossy bank rather than confined to a tidy bed. It tolerates brief dry spells once its rhizomes are established but colors and grows best with consistent moisture and high humidity. Site in zones 8-10 in a sheltered, frost-protected spot, or grow in a container that can be moved under cover in hard freezes.

planting.note: Plant container-grown specimens in spring in moist, humus-rich, acidic, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; rough tree fern forms a slender black trunk topped with a crown of arching fronds and grows faster than most tree ferns given consistent moisture.

directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, acidic, well-drained soil in partial to full shade, sheltered from strong wind and drying sun; rough tree fern is a New Zealand native that develops a narrow, dark, fibrous trunk retaining old dead fronds in a distinctive skirt beneath the live crown unless they are trimmed away. It is among the faster-growing tree ferns in cultivation and tolerates slightly drier and more open conditions than Dicksonia antarctica, though it still needs consistent moisture at the roots and high humidity to look its best. In cold-winter areas it can be grown in a large container and overwintered under cover, or planted outdoors in a sheltered zone 8-10 courtyard with winter mulch over the crown. Underplant with smaller shade ferns and woodland perennials for a layered, subtropical effect.

planting.note: Plant container-grown specimens in spring in moist, humus-rich, acidic, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; golden tree fern develops a notably thick, stout trunk clothed in persistent golden-brown fibrous frond bases.

directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, acidic, well-drained soil in partial to full shade, sheltered from strong wind; golden tree fern is a New Zealand native distinguished by its unusually thick, stout trunk, often wider than other Dicksonia species, densely clothed in persistent golden-brown fibrous frond bases that give the trunk a shaggy, warm-toned appearance. It is among the more cold-tolerant tree ferns and, like its relatives, benefits from winter mulch packed around the crown and trunk base in marginal zones. Its dense, skirted trunk of old fronds provides habitat value and insulation for the growing tip in cold weather; some growers trim the skirt for a tidier look while others leave it for extra frost protection. Underplant with shade perennials and smaller ferns for a layered woodland or subtropical display.

planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in coarse, humus-rich, well-drained substrate in bright indirect light to shade; this cultivar shows wavier, more ruffled frond margins than the plain-leaved species.

directions: Grow in coarse, humus-rich, well-drained substrate in bright indirect light to shade, allowing the surface to dry slightly between waterings as for the species. This selection of blue star fern is distinguished from the plain-leaved form by its more deeply waved and ruffled frond margins, giving an even more textured, decorative silhouette while retaining the same powdery blue-green frond color and creeping, rhizomatous growth habit. Like the species, it is epiphytic in habit and prefers an open, airy, bark-based substrate rather than dense potting soil, and resents prolonged wet feet. Best grown as a container or hanging-basket specimen in frost-free gardens, or as a houseplant in colder zones; protect from temperatures below 50°F.
